check.q: How does the reading say to judge an advertisement?
choices: By the number of facts it cites
By whether it names an expert
By how long it is
By asking what it wants you to feel and whether that feeling relates to what it wants you to do
check.why: Ads pair a claim with a feeling. Naming the trade, friendship for soda, breaks the spell.

check.q: Why did the pediatrician's admission about buses make her column more believable?
choices: It made the column longer
It showed she had thought about the problem
It showed she was dealing honestly with the other side's strongest point
It proved the buses could be changed
check.why: An editorial that faces the best counterargument earns more trust than one that hides it.

check.q: What test does the reading give for a speech?
choices: Ask what would survive if you wrote it down
Count the applause
Check whether the speaker used notes
Time it with a stopwatch
check.why: A speech leans on presence and feeling; writing it down shows how much argument was actually there.

lessons.title: How Good Is the Evidence?
lessons.mainIdea: Evidence is not all equal: ask where it came from, how much of it there is, how recent it is, and whether it actually supports the claim.
reading: Two people tell you a new phone is terrible. One tried it for a day. The other runs a repair shop and has seen five hundred of them. Both are giving you evidence. It is not the same evidence. The first job of a reader is to sort what is offered by its weight, and there are four questions that do most of the sorting. Where did this come from? How much of it is there? How recent is it? And does it actually support the claim it is attached to?

Source first. A statistic from a national study is not the same as a statistic from a company selling the product. An expert in sleep is not an expert in bus schedules. When a text says studies show, ask which studies, and whether you could find them. Then quantity. One story is an *anecdote*: vivid, human, and proof of almost nothing on its own, because one case can always be an exception. Dani's alarm clock was an anecdote. It moved the room, and it was honest, but a thousand students with different alarms would tell you more. The pediatrician's two districts were a small sample too. Good readers notice the number.

Recency matters when the world changes. A study of teenage sleep from twenty years ago may still hold; a statistic about phone use from five years ago probably does not. And then the hardest question: *relevance*. Evidence can be true, plentiful and fresh and still not prove the point. Suppose a column shows that students in a later-starting district earn higher grades. That is real evidence. But if the district is also wealthier, the grades may come from the money, not the clock. The evidence is true; the link to the claim is weak.

Make this a habit with a simple mark. When you read an argument, put a small mark by every piece of evidence and rate it quickly: strong, fair or weak, on those four questions. Then look at what the argument rests on. Some arguments turn out to rest on one strong study and a lot of noise; that is fine, if the study holds. Some rest on nothing but anecdotes and confidence. Those are the ones to be careful with, especially when you agree with them.

words.d: a single short story used as evidence; vivid but not proof on its own
the group of cases an evidence claim is based on
how directly a piece of evidence bears on the claim it is meant to support
a number that summarizes a set of facts or measurements

look.title: Four Pieces of Evidence
look.text: A student argues that the cafeteria should drop its pizza day. Her evidence: (1) her cousin got sick after pizza once; (2) a survey of 12 friends found 9 prefer tacos; (3) a nutrition study from 1994 on frozen pizza; (4) the district's own report that pizza day produces the least food waste of any meal.
look.prompt: Rate each piece of evidence as strong, fair or weak using the four questions. Which piece actually cuts against her claim, and what should she do with it?

check.q: What is an anecdote, as the reading uses the word?
choices: A false story
A joke told in a speech
A statistic from a study
A single story used as evidence, vivid but not proof on its own
check.why: One case is human and memorable, but it can always be an exception.

check.q: Students in a wealthier district with a later start time earn higher grades. Why is this weak evidence that the later start caused the grades?
choices: The evidence is too recent
The money, not the clock, might explain the grades
Grades are not a real measurement
The district is too small to count
check.why: The evidence is true, but another factor could be the real cause, so its relevance to the claim is weak.

check.q: When does the reading say to be most careful about arguments built on anecdotes and confidence?
choices: When they are about food
When they come from experts
When you agree with them
When they are printed in a newspaper
check.why: Agreement lowers a reader's guard, which is exactly when weak evidence slips through.

lessons.title: Finding the Assumption
lessons.mainIdea: Every argument rests on something unstated, and finding that assumption is often the fastest way to test the argument.
reading: Here is a complete argument in two sentences. Teenagers are tired in first period. Therefore school should start later. It sounds finished, but there is a gap between the evidence and the conclusion, and something invisible is bridging it. The bridge is an *assumption*: a belief the argument needs but never states. Here the assumption is that the tiredness comes from the start time and not from something else, such as phones at midnight. If that assumption fails, the evidence stays true and the conclusion falls anyway.

Every argument has assumptions. That is not a flaw; it is how arguments work. Nobody can state everything. The question is whether the assumption is one the audience would accept if it were said aloud. Let Us Sleep assumes that sleep is the school's responsibility. Many people would agree. Some would not, and they would say a student who wants sleep should go to bed. The poster never argues that point because it never sees it. Its readers who disagree are not being stubborn; they are rejecting a premise the poster did not know it had.

To find an assumption, write the evidence on one line and the conclusion on another, and ask what would have to be true for the first to lead to the second. Then say it out loud in the plainest words you can. Often it sounds reasonable, and you move on. Sometimes it sounds like this: all the people in this group think alike. Or: what happened once will happen again. Or: because I want this, it must be true. Said aloud, those collapse. That is why speakers leave them unsaid, sometimes on purpose and often without noticing.

Lincoln in 1858, running for the Senate in Illinois, said that a house divided against itself cannot stand, and that the nation could not remain permanently half slave and half free. His stated evidence was the history of the slavery fight. His assumption, which he made plain, was that the nation would eventually become all one thing or all the other. His opponent Stephen Douglas rejected exactly that assumption, arguing that the states could go on differing forever. The whole campaign was a fight over an unstated premise brought into the open. That is what a good argument does.

words.d: a belief an argument depends on but does not state
a starting statement that an argument builds from
the claim an argument arrives at

look.title: A House Divided
look.text: A house divided against itself cannot stand. I believe this government cannot endure, permanently half slave and half free.
look.cite: Abraham Lincoln, speech accepting the Republican nomination for the Senate, Springfield, Illinois, June 16, 1858
look.prompt: The first sentence is an image, not evidence. What assumption connects the image of a house to the claim about the nation, and how could an opponent attack it?

check.q: What is an assumption in an argument?
choices: A piece of evidence that is false
A belief the argument needs but never states
The final sentence of a speech
A question asked for effect
check.why: An assumption bridges the gap between evidence and conclusion. The argument depends on it even though it is unsaid.

check.q: Why does the reading say readers who disagree with the Let Us Sleep poster are not just being stubborn?
choices: The poster has no website
They are rejecting a premise the poster did not know it had
The photo was not of a real student
They did not read the whole poster
check.why: The poster assumes sleep is the school's responsibility and never argues it; those readers reject that assumption.

check.q: What was the unstated premise that the Lincoln and Douglas campaign brought into the open?
choices: That Illinois should leave the Union
That the Senate should be abolished
That the nation would eventually become all slave or all free
That houses cannot be divided
check.why: Lincoln stated it plainly; Douglas rejected it, arguing that the states could differ forever.

lessons.title: Slippery Slope and Straw Man
lessons.mainIdea: A slippery slope predicts disaster without showing each step; a straw man attacks a weaker version of the other side's argument.
reading: A *fallacy* is a pattern of reasoning that looks like an argument but does not do the work of one. Fallacies are worth naming because they repeat. Once you know the shape, you see it in a board meeting, a comment thread and your own first draft. This lesson and the next two name five of the most common. Learn them as shapes, not as insults; calling someone's point a fallacy without showing where the reasoning breaks is itself a lazy move.

The *slippery slope* says that one step will lead, unstoppably, to a terrible end. If we let students use phones at lunch, next they will use them in class, then during tests, and then no one will learn anything. Each step might follow. But the argument never shows that it must. It skips from the first step to the cliff and lets fear do the rest. The test is simple: ask for the reasons at each step. A real argument can give them. A slippery slope has nothing to say when you ask why the second step follows from the first.

The *straw man* is a different move. Instead of answering what the other side said, the speaker answers something weaker that sounds similar, knocks it down, and takes a bow. The pediatrician asked for a one-year trial of a later start time. A board member replied that we cannot let students sleep until noon. Nobody had asked for noon. The board member built a figure of straw, easy to topple, and toppled it. The test is to go back to the original words. If the reply answers something the other side did not say, it has answered nothing.

Both fallacies are common because both feel like winning. The slippery slope makes the speaker sound like the only one who sees danger; the straw man makes the other side sound foolish. Neither one moves a careful listener, and both leave the real question untouched. When you catch one in your own writing, the fix is the same: go back to the actual claim on the other side, state it in words its holders would accept, and answer that. It is harder. It is also the only thing that works on people who do not already agree with you.

words.d: a pattern of reasoning that looks like an argument but fails to prove its point
claiming one step will lead unstoppably to disaster without showing why each step follows
attacking a weaker version of the other side's argument instead of the real one

look.title: The Comment Thread
look.text: A post says: The library should stay open until 8 on weeknights. First reply: So you want the library open all night and the staff never going home? Second reply: Sure, and then the park will want to stay open, and then every building in town, and taxes will double.
look.prompt: Name the fallacy in each reply, and write the reply a careful person would give instead, one that actually answers the post.

check.q: What is the test for a slippery slope argument?
choices: Check whether the ending is truly terrible
Count the number of steps
See whether it was said in a speech
Ask for the reasons why each step must follow the one before
check.why: A real argument can explain each step; a slippery slope skips from the first step to the cliff.

check.q: The pediatrician asked for a one-year trial. The board member replied that students cannot sleep until noon. What is this?
choices: A slippery slope
A straw man
A fair objection
An anecdote
check.why: The reply answers a weaker claim nobody made, then knocks it down.

check.q: What does the reading say to do when you catch a straw man in your own writing?
choices: Delete the paragraph entirely
Add more evidence for your side
State the other side's real claim in words they would accept, and answer that
Replace it with a rhetorical question
check.why: Answering the actual argument is harder but is the only thing that works on people who do not already agree.

lessons.title: Hasty Generalization and False Cause
lessons.mainIdea: Jumping from too few cases to a rule, or from one thing following another to one thing causing another, are two of the most natural mistakes in reasoning.
reading: You meet two people from a town and both are rude, so the town is rude. A friend fails one quiz and decides she is bad at math. A *hasty generalization* takes a small number of cases and stretches them into a rule about everyone. The mind does this on its own, because patterns are useful and quick. The fallacy is not in noticing a pattern; it is in stopping there. Two cases are a hunch. A rule needs enough cases, chosen fairly, to rule out the chance that you just happened to meet the wrong two.

Watch for the words that hide it: everyone, always, no one, teenagers, people like that. Then look for the sample. In a school debate on start times, a student said that everyone she knew was exhausted by second period. Her sample was her friends, who stayed up together on the same group chat. That is a real observation about a real group. It says nothing about the freshman who goes to bed at nine. Fixing the fallacy does not mean abandoning the claim. It means shrinking it to the size of the evidence: many students I know, not everyone.

*False cause* is a cousin. Because one thing happened after another, the argument says the first caused the second. The district moved its start time and test scores rose; therefore the start time raised the scores. Maybe. But the same year the district hired new teachers and cut class sizes. The order of events proves nothing by itself. The classic case: ice cream sales and drownings both rise in July, and neither one causes the other; summer causes both. Whenever you see after, therefore because of, look for the third thing.

Both fallacies are the raw material of most bad arguments about people. Almost every prejudice is a hasty generalization, and almost every superstition is a false cause. That is why they matter beyond essays. The habit that guards against them is a single question, asked before you believe and before you write: what else could explain this? If you can think of one other cause or one exception, you do not have a proof yet. You have a lead, and a lead is worth following, honestly.

words.d: drawing a rule about a whole group from too few cases
assuming that because one thing followed another, the first caused the second
a statement about a whole group based on some of its members

look.title: Two Things That Rise Together
rows: January: ice cream cones sold at a lake stand
look.cite: model figures written for this lesson to show a seasonal pattern; not real sales data
look.prompt: Swimming accidents at the same lake also peak in July. What third thing explains both patterns, and what would someone claim who fell for the false-cause fallacy?

check.q: Which sentence is a hasty generalization?
choices: I met two people from Rockford and both were rude, so Rockford is a rude town.
Most of the twenty students I surveyed preferred a later start.
The study followed 3,000 students for two years.
Some drivers on this road speed.
check.why: Two cases are stretched into a rule about a whole town.

check.q: Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in July. What does the reading say is the real explanation?
choices: Ice cream causes cramps
Drowning news makes people buy ice cream
It is a coincidence with no cause
A third thing, summer, causes both
check.why: When two things rise together, look for the third thing before assuming one caused the other.

check.q: How does the reading say to fix a hasty generalization without abandoning the claim?
choices: Add more emotion to it
Say it more confidently
Shrink the claim to the size of the evidence
Replace it with a story
check.why: Many students I know is a claim the evidence supports; everyone is not.

lessons.title: Appeal to Authority and Other Shortcuts
lessons.mainIdea: Citing an authority is fine when the authority is real and relevant; it becomes a fallacy when the name replaces the reasoning.
reading: A doctor says the start time should change. A famous athlete says the same. Which one counts? Both are appeals to authority, and one of them is legitimate. The doctor is an expert on the thing being argued, sleep and adolescent health, and her expertise is a reason to weigh her view. The athlete is an expert on running, which is not the question. The *appeal to authority* becomes a fallacy when the authority is outside the field, when the authority is unnamed, or when a name is used to end the discussion instead of to add to it.

The test has two parts. Is this person actually an expert on this exact question? And does the argument still show its reasoning, or does it stop at the name? Studies show, experts agree and everyone knows are the sound of the second failure. A real expert can be cited and then checked. A vague one cannot. Notice, too, that even a true expert can be wrong; the appeal gives you a reason to listen, not a reason to stop thinking. Aristotle was a genuine authority, and he thought heavy objects fall faster than light ones.

A few other shortcuts are worth naming because they appear so often. The *ad hominem* attacks the person instead of the argument: of course she wants a later start, she is a teenager. The *bandwagon* says a thing is true because many people believe it. The *false dilemma* offers only two choices when there are more: either we change the start time or we accept failing students. Each of these can be answered the same way. Bring the conversation back to the claim and the evidence, which is where it should have been.

One warning. Learning the names of fallacies can make a reader feel clever and go hunting, and a hunt for fallacies is not the same as a search for the truth. An argument with a fallacy in it may still be right; the fallacy just means that particular step did not prove it. The right response is not to declare victory but to ask what evidence would prove the point, and then to look for it. Fallacies are places where the work was skipped. The work still has to be done, by someone.

words.d: supporting a claim by citing an expert; a fallacy when the expert is irrelevant, vague or used in place of reasoning
attacking the person making an argument instead of the argument itself
presenting only two options when more exist
arguing that something is true because many people believe it

look.title: Five Sentences from a Board Meeting

(4) A famous quarterback says teens need more sleep. (5) A 2014 statement from the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30.
look.prompt: Name the shortcut in each of the first four. What makes the fifth different, and what would you still want to check about it?

check.q: When is an appeal to authority legitimate, according to the reading?
choices: When the authority is famous
When the authority is named, is an expert on the exact question, and the reasoning is still shown
When the authority agrees with you
Never; all appeals to authority are fallacies
check.why: A real, relevant expert who can be checked adds weight. The fallacy is using a name instead of reasoning.

check.q: Of course she wants a later start, she is a teenager. Which shortcut is this?
choices: Bandwagon
False dilemma
Ad hominem
Slippery slope
check.why: It attacks the person making the argument instead of the argument.

check.q: What warning does the reading give about learning the names of fallacies?
choices: The names are too hard to remember
Hunting for fallacies is not the same as searching for the truth
Fallacies only appear in speeches
An argument with a fallacy is always wrong
check.why: A fallacy means one step skipped the work; the point may still be right, and the work still has to be done.

lessons.title: The Rhetorical Situation of a Feed
lessons.mainIdea: Social media is a rhetorical situation with its own audience, purpose and pressures, and those pressures reward the weakest kinds of argument.
reading: Apply the four questions from the last chapter to a post in your feed. Who is speaking? Often you cannot tell, and the name might be invented. To whom? To everyone and no one, since the writer does not know who will see it. Why? Frequently to be seen, shared and liked, which is a different purpose from persuading. When? In a stream that moves so fast that a post has a few seconds to earn a second look. That is the *rhetorical situation* of social media, and it explains a great deal about what appears there.

The pressures of that situation reward certain moves. Short claims beat long reasoning, because reasoning takes room. Strong feeling beats careful evidence, because feeling travels faster than checking. Certainty beats doubt, because no one shares a post that says it might be complicated. A straw man is easy to write and easy to cheer. A slippery slope fits in one line. The feed is not full of fallacies because people online are foolish. It is full of them because the form rewards them, the way a poster rewards a slogan.

That has consequences for readers. The post that reaches you has already been sorted by how much feeling it produced in other people, not by how true it was. Your own feed is also shaped by what you have clicked, so it learns to show you the arguments you already like. That is a hasty generalization machine: you see the same kind of case a hundred times and conclude that the world is like that. The fix is not to leave the feed. It is to read it knowing what it is, the way you read an ad knowing what it is.

The most useful habit is to take a post you feel strongly about and treat it as a text. Write down the claim. Write down the evidence, if any. Name the appeal it leans on. Look for the assumption. Ask what form it is, an ad, an anecdote, an argument, and hold it to that form's standard. Three minutes of this on a post that made you angry will usually show you that the post was built to make you angry, which is a different thing from being right.

words.d: the stream of posts a social media app shows a user, sorted by the app
to pass a post along so that others see it
a tone of complete confidence, with no room for doubt

look.title: Two Posts, One Study
look.text: Post A: New study PROVES later school start times raise grades. Share if you agree. Post B: A study of two districts found grades rose after a later start; the authors say other changes that year may have contributed. Post A was shared eleven thousand times. Post B was shared forty.
look.prompt: Which post is more accurate, and which is built for the feed? What single change would make Post A honest, and would it still travel?

check.q: Why does the reading say a feed is full of fallacies?
choices: Because the form rewards short, certain, emotional claims
Because people online are foolish
Because no experts use social media
Because posts are not allowed to cite sources
check.why: The rhetorical situation of a feed favors the moves that travel fastest, and those are the weakest kinds of argument.

check.q: Why does the reading call a feed a hasty generalization machine?
choices: It shows posts in random order
It only shows posts from strangers
It deletes posts that are too long
It shows you the same kind of case over and over until you conclude the world is like that
check.why: A feed learns what you click and repeats it, so a small sample looks like everyone.

check.q: What is the first step in the habit the reading recommends for a post you feel strongly about?
choices: Reply to it immediately
Share it with a comment
Write down the claim and then the evidence
Block the writer
check.why: Treating the post as a text, claim first, is how you find out whether it was built to be right or built to make you angry.

lessons.title: Checking Before You Share
lessons.mainIdea: Sharing a claim is making it, so check the source, the date and the original context before passing it on.
reading: When you share a post, you become its author for everyone who sees it through you. That is the plain rhetorical fact. If it is wrong, you said it. So the question before sharing is the same as the question before writing: can I stand behind this? A few checks take less time than typing a comment. They are the checks a good editor makes before printing a letter, and they are worth learning as a habit rather than a rule.

First, find the source. A screenshot of a headline is not a source; the article is. A post that says a study found is not a source; the study is. Click through, and if there is nothing to click through to, that silence is the answer. Second, check the date. Old news gets shared as new all the time, and a true statistic from 2015 can be a false one now. Third, check the *context*: the words around the words. A quotation cut out of a speech can mean the opposite of what the speech meant, and irony, as the last chapter showed, dies the moment it leaves its context.

Fourth, look sideways. Instead of reading more of the post, open a new tab and see what other, independent sources say about the same claim. If a startling fact appears in only one place, that is a reason for doubt, not excitement. If the same claim is being made by sources that do not usually agree, it is more likely to be true. This is the habit of a reporter, and it is faster than it sounds once it is a habit.

Finally, notice your own feeling. The posts you most want to share are the ones that made you feel something strongly, and that feeling is exactly what a weak argument counts on. This does not mean distrusting everything that moves you. It means that a strong feeling is a signal to check, the way a car's warning light is a signal to look under the hood. Douglass's speech moves people to this day, and every fact in it holds. Being moved and being right are not enemies. They just have to be checked separately.

words.d: the original place a piece of information came from
the words and situation surrounding a statement that give it its meaning
not connected to or controlled by the same people

look.title: The Screenshot
look.text: A friend sends you a screenshot of a headline: District cuts all music classes. No link, no date, no newspaper name visible. Under it your friend has written: this is why I'm done with this town. You have the phone in your hand and a thumb over the share button.
look.prompt: List the four checks from the reading in the order you would do them for this screenshot. Which one would most likely settle it, and what would you say to your friend?

check.q: Why does the reading say sharing a post is like writing it?
choices: Because sharing takes as long as writing
Because the app labels shared posts with your name
Because everyone who sees it through you is hearing it from you
Because shared posts cannot be deleted
check.why: For your audience, you are the author of what you pass on, and you are responsible for it.

check.q: A startling claim appears in only one place online. What does the reading say this should mean to a reader?
choices: The claim is a scoop and should be shared quickly
The claim is a reason for doubt, not excitement
The claim must be true because no one has argued with it
The claim is probably a joke
check.why: Looking sideways at independent sources is the check; one lonely source fails it.

check.q: What does the reading say a strong feeling about a post should be treated as?
choices: A sign the post is false
A sign the post is true
A reason to share it immediately
A signal to check, like a warning light
check.why: Being moved and being right are separate; the feeling is a cue to look under the hood.

lessons.title: Anticipating the Objection
lessons.mainIdea: A strong written argument states the best objection to itself fairly and answers it, which is called a counterclaim and rebuttal.
reading: Picture the reader who disagrees with you, sitting across the table, arms folded. Every argument you write is really addressed to that person; the ones who already agree do not need convincing. So the most important paragraph in an argument is the one where you say what that reader is thinking. Writers call it the *counterclaim*: the strongest point on the other side, stated in words its holders would accept. Then comes the *rebuttal*: your answer to it. An argument without those two is a speech to an empty room.

The counterclaim must be the strong version. The pediatrician's column did this well. It did not say some people worry about small problems like buses. It said that a later start would push the end of the day later, that buses serve three schools on one schedule, that after-school jobs and practices would be squeezed, and that these were real costs to real families. Only after that did it answer: a one-year trial would show whether the costs were as high as feared, and other districts had solved the bus problem by staggering routes. A reader with folded arms unfolds them a little when she hears her own point stated better than she would have stated it.

There are three honest ways to rebut. You can show the objection rests on a mistake of fact. You can concede that it is true but show that your point outweighs it. Or you can concede it fully and narrow your claim. That last one feels like losing and is often winning: a smaller claim that survives is worth more than a large one that does not. What you cannot do is rebut a straw man, ignore the objection, or bury it in the last sentence with a quick but. Readers notice, and they stop trusting everything above it.

Here is the shape of an argument that survives contact. A claim, stated exactly. Two or three pieces of evidence, each rated strong by the four questions. The reasoning that links them, with the assumption stated when it matters. The counterclaim in its strongest form. The rebuttal. And a conclusion that says what should happen now. Write the counterclaim paragraph first, before the rest of the draft. If you cannot state it fairly, you do not understand the question well enough to argue about it yet.

words.d: the strongest point on the opposing side, stated fairly within your own argument
your answer to a counterclaim
to admit that a point on the other side is true

look.title: A Counterclaim Paragraph
look.text: The strongest case against a later start is not laziness or tradition; it is the bus. Our district runs one fleet for three schools, and if the high school moves, an elementary school moves too, and some six-year-olds will wait in the dark. That is a real cost, and any proposal that pretends otherwise deserves to fail. Two neighboring districts, though, solved it by staggering routes, and a one-year trial would show whether we can.
look.cite: model paragraph written for this lesson
look.prompt: Find the counterclaim, the concession and the rebuttal. Which of the three honest ways of rebutting does this paragraph use?

check.q: What is a counterclaim?
choices: The main claim of an argument
A claim with no evidence
A weak version of the opposing view
The strongest opposing point, stated fairly within your own argument
check.why: A counterclaim must be the strong version, in words the other side would accept.

check.q: Which of these is one of the three honest ways to rebut, according to the reading?
choices: Concede the point fully and narrow your claim
Bury the objection in the last sentence with a quick but
Restate the objection in a weaker form
Skip the objection and add more evidence
check.why: Narrowing a claim feels like losing but often wins, because a smaller claim that survives is worth more.

check.q: Why does the reading say to write the counterclaim paragraph first?
choices: Because it is the shortest paragraph
Because if you cannot state it fairly, you do not yet understand the question
Because readers only read the first paragraph
Because it contains the thesis
check.why: Stating the other side well is the test of whether you are ready to argue at all.

lessons.title: Disagreeing Well
lessons.mainIdea: Civil disagreement is not softness; it is a set of moves that keep the argument on the claim and give the other person a reason to keep listening.
reading: Two students disagree about a book. One says the ending was a cheat. The other says the ending was the only honest one. Ten minutes later they are talking about who always interrupts. The argument has left the book and moved to the people, and from there it can only get worse. *Civil disagreement* is the skill of keeping an argument on the claim. It is not about being polite for its own sake. It is about the fact that ad hominem, once it starts, ends every chance of anyone changing their mind.

The first move is to say back what the other person said before answering it. I think you are saying the ending was honest because the character had been lying to himself the whole book, is that right? This does three things. It proves you listened. It catches misunderstandings before they grow. And it forces you to build the steel version of their point instead of the straw one. Most disagreements that go bad go bad because each side is answering something the other did not say.

The second move is to separate the claim from the person. She is wrong about the ending, not she always thinks she is right. The third move is to name what you agree on. Two people who agree that the character was lying to himself, and disagree only about whether the ending should have punished him, have shrunk the fight to something that can be settled. The fourth move is to change your mind out loud when you should. It is the rarest thing in an argument, and the most persuasive, because it shows the other person that changing their mind would not be a defeat either.

The philosopher John Stuart Mill argued in 1859 that a person who knows only their own side of a case knows little even of that side, because the reasons for a position only become clear when you have heard the strongest case against it. That is the deepest reason for civil disagreement. The person across the table is not only an opponent. They are the only source of the objections your own argument needs. Treat them like that, and the argument becomes something two people do together rather than something one does to the other.

words.d: arguing about a claim while keeping the argument off the people making it
to restate someone's point in your own words
the points two sides in a disagreement already agree on

look.title: Knowing Only Your Own Side
look.text: In On Liberty, Mill argues that someone who knows only their own side of a case knows little of that. Their reasons may be good, and no one may have refuted them, but if they cannot refute the reasons on the opposite side, and do not even know what those reasons are, they have no ground for preferring either opinion.
look.cite: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, 1859 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Mill says you do not really understand your own view until you can state the best case against it. Test that on something you believe strongly. Can you make the other side's case?

check.q: What is the first move in disagreeing well, according to the reading?
choices: State your own claim as strongly as possible
Say back what the other person said before answering it
Find something they got wrong
Change the subject to common ground
check.why: Restating their point proves you listened, catches misunderstandings, and builds the strong version of their view.

check.q: Why does the reading call changing your mind out loud the most persuasive move?
choices: It ends the argument quickly
It proves you were right all along
It shows the other person that changing their mind would not be a defeat
It makes the other person feel guilty
check.why: When one person visibly moves, the other learns that moving is safe.

check.q: What is Mill's reason that a person who knows only their own side knows little of it?
choices: Reasons for a position only become clear against the strongest case on the other side
Most people are wrong about most things
Arguments should be avoided
Only experts should hold opinions
check.why: Without the best objections, you cannot know why your reasons hold, or whether they do.

lessons.title: A Structured Debate
lessons.mainIdea: A formal debate gives each side equal time, a fixed order and a duty to answer, which forces the moves this chapter has taught.
reading: In 1858 Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas held seven debates across Illinois, in towns from Ottawa to Alton, before crowds of thousands. The format was strict. The first speaker had an hour. The second had an hour and a half. Then the first had thirty minutes to reply. Nobody could dodge, because the other man would be standing there in a few minutes with the crowd listening. The format did not make the two men honest. It made dishonesty expensive, which is the most a format can do.

A classroom *debate* borrows that idea at a smaller scale. A *resolution* is stated, a sentence that can be argued for or against: this school should start at 8:30. One side affirms it, the other opposes. Each side gives an opening with its claim and best evidence. Then comes the part that matters, the *rebuttal* round, where each side must answer what the other actually said. Then closings. A judge or the class scores not who was loudest but who answered the other side's strongest point and who left it standing.

Preparing for a debate is the best practice in this chapter, because you do not know which side you will get. You have to build the strongest case for both. That means finding the best evidence for each and rating it with the four questions. It means locating the assumptions. It means predicting the other side's counterclaims, so that your rebuttal is ready before they speak. Students who prepare only their own side lose to students who prepared both, every time. The second group has already heard every point the first group will make.

Rules for the room, written for this lesson. Speak to the claim, never to the person. Say back the point before you answer it. Cite evidence by its source, and expect to be asked where it came from. Concede what is true; the judge will notice, and it costs you nothing. Keep time. And when it ends, shake hands, because the person across from you just gave you the objections your argument needed, and next week you may be arguing their side.

words.d: a formal argument with two sides, fixed order and equal time
the statement a debate argues for or against
to argue in favor of the resolution
the round in which each side answers the other side's arguments

look.title: Time in a Lincoln-Douglas Debate, 1858
look.cite: format of the seven Lincoln-Douglas debates, Illinois, 1858
look.prompt: Each speaker gets ninety minutes total. Why might the organizers have split the time this way instead of giving each man one ninety-minute speech?

check.q: What does the reading say a strict debate format actually does?
choices: It guarantees that both speakers tell the truth
It makes the audience quieter
It gives the better speaker more time
It makes dishonesty expensive, since the other side will answer in minutes
check.why: The format cannot make people honest, but it makes dodging costly in front of a crowd.

check.q: What is a resolution in a debate?
choices: The judge's final decision
The closing speech
The statement one side affirms and the other opposes
A rule about time limits
check.why: The resolution is the sentence being argued, such as this school should start at 8:30.

check.q: Why does the reading say to prepare both sides of a debate?
choices: Students who prepare both sides have already heard every point the other side will make
The judge will ask you to switch sides
It takes less time than preparing one side
Rules require it
check.why: Building the strongest case for both sides means no counterclaim surprises you.

review.q: Which form of persuasive text should a reader most expect to contain checkable evidence?
choices: A poster
A slogan
An editorial
A song
review.why: An editorial has room for evidence, so its absence there is a warning.

review.q: Which of the four questions about evidence asks whether the evidence actually bears on the claim?
choices: Where did it come from?
How much is there?
How recent is it?
Is it relevant?
review.why: Evidence can be true, plentiful and fresh and still fail to support the point.

choices: That the tiredness comes from the start time rather than something else
That teenagers do not like school
That school should end earlier
That first period is the hardest class
review.why: The bridge between evidence and conclusion is the assumption that the start time is the cause.

review.q: If we allow one club to sell snacks, soon every class will be a store and no one will learn. What fallacy is this?
choices: Straw man
Ad hominem
False dilemma
Slippery slope
review.why: It leaps from one step to disaster without showing why each step must follow.

choices: Hasty generalization
False cause
Appeal to authority
Bandwagon
review.why: One thing followed another; that does not mean the first caused the second.

review.q: Why does a social media feed reward weak arguments, according to the chapter?
choices: Because strong arguments are banned
Because most users are young
Because the form favors short, certain, emotional claims that travel fast
Because posts cannot include links
review.why: The rhetorical situation of a feed, seconds to earn a look and sorting by feeling, favors the weakest moves.

choices: Ignore it
Restate it in a weaker form
Bury it with a quick but
Concede it fully and narrow your claim
review.why: A smaller claim that survives is worth more than a large one that does not.

choices: The opening
The rebuttal
The resolution
The closing
